newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean defector to leave Beijing this week-Seoul.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector to leave Beijing this week-Seoul.

text.p: North Korea's top ideologue, languishing in Seoul's mission in Beijing, will fly to a third country this week after China and South Korea hammer out fine details of his departure, Seoul officials said.
There was no end to the nearly five-week diplomatic impasse over the fate of Hwang Jang-yop, despite a flurry of reports that he had been spirited out of the heavily guarded consulate.

Three vans seen driving away from Beijing's embassy district in the early hours of Monday, following a visit to the consulate by South Korean ambassador Chung Chong-wook on Sunday night, touched off a false alarm, one Seoul official said.
"Hwang Jang-yop will be able to leave China this week but his departure might not be today or tomorrow," a senior foreign ministry official, who declined to be identified, told reporters.
"He will have to stay in a third country for a considerable period of time before coming to South Korea."
Hwang, the most senior North Korean official to flee the troubled communist state, has been stranded in the consulate since arriving with an aide on February 12 and seeking asylum.
Beijing has been grappling with the problem of how to hand over Hwang to new business partner Seoul while appearing to give consideration to the concerns of old communist ally Pyongyang.
The foreign ministry official declined to identify Hwang's likely first stop, saying an announcement would be made once Hwang arrived.
He said the Philippines was one of several "transit points" being considered.

South Korea's state radio said Hwang was expected to spend a month in Subic Bay, a former U.S. naval base north of Manila and now a free port with an international airport, before being brought to South Korea.
Chinese police armed with assault rifles were posted at approaches to the consulate. Several armoured personnel carriers and a crowd control truck were parked outside the building.

China's Foreign Ministry refused to comment on Hwang's fate, saying it could report no new developments since Premier Li Peng said last Friday that conditions were nearly ripe for a solution to the diplomatic crisis.
Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said on Saturday his country had been asked to serve as a transit point for Hwang if he were allowed to leave for South Korea.
Siazon, now on a five-day visit to Tokyo, told reporters on Monday that some other routes besides the Philippines were probably being considered.
A top Manila Foreign Office official said Hwang would very likely stay in the Philippines for a few days, but added that it was possible his country was being used as a decoy.
Hwang, a close aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, is ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy.
He is credited with devising the national creed of "juche", which stresses self-reliance and has kept North Korea frozen in Stalinist-era isolation and economic backwardness.
